title: Why Did Patagonia's Future Founder Urge Fewer Pitons in 1972?
description:
Why did a 1972 equipment catalog urge customers to use fewer of the company's own pitons? From first-hand recollections of hand forging, through scarred cracks, catalog debates and a big-wall climb, we enter the factory recorded in a later report.

1977 is only the interview article's publication year, not a confirmed visit date. Illustrations are generated by AI and are anonymous conceptual depictions; they do not recreate real people or actual routes.

c09r001.text: An equipment article gave an example: an experienced rope team could place and retrieve up to 100 pitons in a day.

c09r002.text: If you climb that crack next, they may take their pitons away but leave holes widened by repeated hammering for you.

c09r003.text: Imagine opening a 1972 equipment catalog, with a steel piton just pulled from a crack beside you.

c09r004.text: Equipment seller Chouinard later founded Patagonia; in his own catalog, he urged customers to use fewer pitons.

c09r005.text: I think the hardest part comes later: a climb without pitons, and a machine still running in the factory.

c09r006.text: This time, follow one piton to understand this equipment company's choices.

c09r007.text: Why would a piton seller urge you to hammer less, and what later happened to the product he cautioned about?

c09r008.text: Imagine opening an equipment bag from that era: its soft-iron pitons were tools climbers packed for long routes.

c09r009.text: Early soft-iron pitons were not meant for repeated use. Long-route climbers carried dozens and felt every bit of the weight.

c09r010.text: In 1946, another blacksmith made hard-steel pitons that could be retrieved and reused; this precedent was not Chouinard's invention.

c09r011.text: A bag of metal could move up with you, pitch by pitch, lightening the load. But where could you buy these pitons?

c09r012.text: But Chouinard later told the reporter that by 1957, his predecessor's pitons were unavailable and hardly anyone in the US made such gear.

c09r013.text: If you could not buy suitable gear, you might ask another shop. He bought a coal forge and an anvil, learning from books.

c09r014.text: He recalled loading the forge and anvil into his car, stopping along the California coast to light the fire and forge. Working alone, how many could he make an hour?

c09r015.text: Only two, he said. Sometimes he spent all day at the forge; this was no machine dropping out a box at a button's touch.

c09r016.text: He took finished pitons to climbing areas and sold directly to climbers. What price did he ask for this slow handiwork?

c09r017.text: He recalled European pitons costing about US$0.30, while his cost US$1.50 each. Buyers first balked, then gradually accepted the price.

c09r018.text: I find that gap interesting: he sold a small piece of metal, but buyers had to ask whether it was worth taking onto the wall.

c09r040.text: British climbers already used metal chocks. How did this tool, which Chouinard did not invent, differ from pitons?

c09r041.text: A chock wedges into a crack by its shape and can usually be recovered after climbing, avoiding the hammer-in and pull-out process.

c09r043.text: The reporter wrote that Chouinard had already used chocks in 1959 and 1960.

c09r019.text: He said he sold pitons in climbing areas in summer, stocking up in winter for the next summer. What warning did even a price list need?

c09r020.text: In 1964, the first mail-order catalog was one mimeographed price sheet, warning: do not expect fast delivery from May through September.

c09r021.text: The reporter explained that this was climbing season. You see, even delivery speed followed the equipment maker's rhythm of life.

c09r022.text: But the business grew, and handwork could not meet demand. Could an anvil alone deliver what customers wanted?

c09r023.text: Not an anvil alone. They turned to machines and dies; his partner's aeronautical engineering studies helped with die design.

c09r024.text: In 1966, the workshop was set up beside the railway in Ventura; that was also where the reporter later visited the company.

c09r025.text: More pitons were made and became easier to use. That sounds good to buyers, so how did trouble grow from it?

c09r026.text: In 1967, Chouinard and his partner wrote an article on piton use,

c09r027.text: recording how climbers placed and removed them.

c09r029.text: It sorted pitons by size and discussed carrying them for quick access to the right one, with less fumbling on the wall.

c09r030.text: The two authors even called smooth placement and retrieval a mature skill. People used tools better; what about the rock?

c09r044.text: The report quoted a 1970 reply reproduced in a climbing book: he said chocks were useful,

c09r045.text: but would not normally replace pitons.

c09r031.text: But look from the hands to the crack, and the same act has another cost: people retrieve the piton; rock takes the hammer blow.

c09r032.text: One party follows another. All reuse their own tools on the same crack, again and again. What is left on the wall?

c09r033.text: The 1972 catalog preface says repeated hammering and removal left rows of piton holes in popular Yosemite routes.

c09r034.text: Remember the opening crack? Alloy steel is harder than granite; thin flakes may also loosen and break off during hammering and removal.

c09r035.text: Reading this, I feel that "reusable" is incomplete:

c09r036.text: you can bring the piton back, but when the crack widens, will the original small piton still work?

c09r037.text: The report adds that some cracks had outgrown the original small pitons, forcing later climbers to use larger ones. Tools changed with the scars.

c09r038.text: That next climber could be you. The gear in your backpack is yours; the rock before you carries everyone else's earlier choices.

c09r039.text: Remember the chock? Both tools can be retrieved; now the cost to the rock makes their difference more concrete.

c09r042.text: But cracks have different conditions; changing tools is no safety guarantee.

c09r046.text: Remember the widened crack? He said he once thought climbing did not harm rock. Where did he write this discovery?

c09r047.text: Back to the opening catalog, their advice was: on suitable routes,

c09r048.text: consider removable chocks first. The products now came with an order of preference.

c09r049.text: The preface says mountains are not inexhaustible, and even the company's own gear should be used with restraint. So how does it judge a climb's success?

c09r050.text: Not only by reaching the top, but by how you climb. What I find most unusual

c09r051.text: is that the tool seller began asking you to consider whether to strike that blow.

c09r052.text: But at the foot of a wall with a hammer, does reading "show restraint" tell you what to choose next?

c09r053.text: No. Beyond advice, the catalog had to offer customers new choices. The preface first distinguished the conditions of different routes.

c09r054.text: Keep routes already climbed without pitons that way;

c09r055.text: on other suitable routes, try removable chocks first, in that order, rather than treating every crack alike.

c09r056.text: If truly necessary, the preface says fixed pitons can be considered to reduce repeated hammering and removal. But how will later climbers know they are there?

c09r057.text: Their positions must also go in the local climbing guide. Leaving equipment means leaving information for those who follow.

c09r058.text: I think the difficulty remains after you close the booklet: is the preface enough to learn a different tool?

c09r060.text: The catalog then invited another climbing writer to contribute a long essay on climbing without pitons.

c09r061.text: The preface explained why to change; the essay taught how to change equipment.

c09r062.text: A 1973 review lists this catalog as 72 pages.

c09r063.text: The early single-sheet price list had become a booklet with room for a long essay.

c09r064.text: You might ask: is this more than a fine ideal? What could the authors use to show customers that equipment choices make a difference?

c09r065.text: The preface also cites old British routes: footholds were worn smooth, but protection cracks stayed intact because no pitons had been hammered there.

c09r068.text: But the booklet was selling gear too. You turn to its call for restraint,

c09r069.text: then see the prices. Would a thought cross your mind?

c09r070.text: Back to that opening catalog: after reading this advice, would you trust the seller, or think they said one thing and did another?

c09r071.text: The review records just that criticism: Chouinard sold pitons while disparaging them.

c09r072.text: That is an accusation recorded in a review, not an admission of the company's motives. But I think it hits the point buyers find hardest to trust.

c09r073.text: Others wondered about those who had first climbed hard routes using pitons:

c09r074.text: what right did they have to tell later climbers to change tools? Your climbing choices should not be made for you.

c09r075.text: Another question was more direct: if you followed his advice and took no pitons onto a big wall, could you even finish the route?

c09r076.text: The reviewer also described the opposite scene: in Yosemite, he met more people wanting to climb without hammers. That was his observation.

c09r077.text: He rejected the hypocrisy charge, believing the catalog really devoted space to teaching customers how to hammer less.

c09r078.text: But that was the reviewer's judgment. On an actual big wall, what was in Chouinard and his partner's bags?

c09r079.text: Here is the no-piton climb from our opening: that same year, Chouinard and his partner took chocks up a famous long route on El Capitan.

c09r080.text: They completed the climb. "Without" means without pitons, not ropes or other climbing equipment.

c09r082.text: I take that climb as an answer for that route alone, not a guarantee for every wall.

c09r093.text: The brand's retrospective says outdoor clothing began carrying the Patagonia label in 1973.

c09r084.text: Our opening factory question remains: what was that machine doing later?

c09r085.text: In the report published in 1977, the journalist enters the Ventura shop and sees a small display of old pitons.

c09r086.text: Both the earlier blacksmith's pitons and Chouinard's early handmade ones had become exhibits.

c09r087.text: Pitons and chocks were still in the equipment display. You might still wonder: was this old stock, or was the factory actually still making them?

c09r088.text: In the factory behind it, his early portable forge stood idle,

c09r089.text: but a machine kept pressing metal into new pitons. The old tool rested; the product was more than a memory.

c09r090.text: Elsewhere, chocks were wedged into a wooden board resembling a rock wall,

c09r091.text: bright cord loops ran through the gear. The new approach also had a concrete demonstration.

c09r092.text: Remember that clothing label? I find this even more interesting: what did clothing have to do with the equipment factory?

c09r095.text: Chouinard said clothing income subsidized climbing equipment. How much did a die for pressing pitons cost?

c09r096.text: He also said piton-pressing dies cost thousands of dollars,

c09r097.text: estimating that recouping the cost could sometimes take 5 to 10 years. The equipment business had its own difficulties.

c09r098.text: That was his estimate, not an independent financial report.

c09r100.text: Back to the preface's choice: consider not just how often you can reuse a piton, but what crack the next climber inherits.

c09r102.text: Back to that press: the record's answer is that the recommended priorities changed, but the product remained; its seller also began asking whether you should use it.

c09r103.text: If a seller urged you to use less of their own product, would you trust them more, or want to ask why? Tell me in the comments.

c09r104.text: To explore these less clear-cut choices behind familiar brands together, subscribe to this channel.
